items.title: Level 5: Offer, notice and timing decisions
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Most of the practical choices around a new job come from one idea: a conditional offer is not final until the checks are complete. This has several consequences. You should not hand in your notice until you have written confirmation that the checks are cleared and a start date is set. If you must give notice earlier, for example because your contract needs a long notice period, ask the recruitment team for an honest estimate of timing and think about the risk, since you could be left without work if the offer fell through. Replies to requests should be quick, because a start date depends on a complete set of evidence. If a document will take time to obtain, say so at once and ask what the department can accept in the meantime. Do not make financial commitments that depend on the start date until it is confirmed. If your current employer asks for a reference, ask the recruitment team whether it has been requested, so that you do not tell your employer too early. When the date is confirmed, check the contract, the place of work, the hours and the pay before you sign. If you spot an error, raise it before you start. If delays continue with no explanation, politely ask the recruitment contact for an update rather than assuming the offer has gone. Throughout, you act in good faith: you give honest answers, keep your word on dates and keep the department informed if anything changes on your side, such as a new address or a different contact number.

questions.prompt: You have a conditional offer but the checks are not finished. Your employer wants your notice date. What is the best approach?

options.text: Give notice now and ask the department to speed up your checks as a result
Wait for written confirmation that the checks are cleared and a start date is set
Give notice now, because a conditional offer is almost certain to become final
Give notice, but tell your employer that you may return if the offer is withdrawn

questions.hint: The offer is not final until the checks are complete, so you protect your income by waiting.

questions.prompt: Your contract at your current job requires a long notice period. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Ask the recruitment team for an honest estimate of timing and weigh up the risk
Give the full notice at once and assume the checks will be quick
Ask your current employer to shorten your notice period, without explaining why you are asking
Ignore the notice period and leave on the date the department prefers

questions.hint: You need real information about timing to decide, and you should accept that the risk exists.

questions.prompt: A document you need will take three weeks to arrive. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the team only when they chase you for the missing item
Send a photocopy of an older document and hope it is enough
Wait until it arrives and then send everything together, so the pack is complete and tidy
Tell the checks team straight away and ask what they can accept in the meantime

questions.hint: Early information lets the team plan and suggest alternatives.

questions.prompt: Your start date has not been confirmed, but you are about to sign a lease that depends on your salary. What is the better choice?

options.text: Sign the lease and ask the department to bring forward your start date
Sign the lease, because the department has said you are the preferred candidate
Delay big commitments until the start date is confirmed in writing
Sign the lease and tell your landlord that the job is guaranteed

questions.hint: The offer can still change, so financial commitments should wait for a confirmed date.

questions.prompt: The contract you receive shows a different working pattern from the one in the advert. What do you do?

options.text: Cross out the line yourself and sign the rest
Raise it with HR before you sign and before you start
Start work and see whether anyone mentions it
Sign it now and sort out the difference after your first week

questions.hint: Errors are best fixed before signing.

questions.prompt: Three weeks pass with no news from the checks team. What is the best step?

options.text: Send repeated messages every day until you get a reply
Assume the offer has gone and apply elsewhere without telling anyone
Politely ask the recruitment contact for an update
Contact each of your referees and ask them to chase

questions.hint: A courteous enquiry is reasonable and avoids wrong assumptions.

questions.prompt: You move house during the checks period. What should you do?

options.text: Wait to mention it at your first induction meeting
Tell the checks team about your new address as soon as you can
Keep it to yourself until the checks are over, to avoid confusion
Update only your bank, which will pass it on

questions.hint: Changes in contact details need to reach the team so messages and records stay right.

questions.prompt: Your current employer asks for the name of your new employer. What is the sensible response?

options.text: Refuse to say anything and stop attending work until the offer is confirmed
Tell them everything about the new offer immediately, because honesty with your current employer matters most
Check with the recruitment team before you share details about the offer
Name a different department so as to protect your new job

questions.hint: Because the offer is conditional, you should be careful about what you reveal and when.

questions.prompt: You are asked to sign a contract before the start date is confirmed in writing. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Sign now, because the start date can be agreed once you are in the job
Sign now and write the date you expect in the margin yourself
Refuse to sign anything until the day you start work
Ask HR to confirm the start date in writing first and sign once it is clear

questions.hint: A clear written start date avoids later confusion.

items.title: Level 5: Identity document problems
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Identity problems are common and almost always solvable if raised early. Here are the principles for the usual situations. If your name differs between documents, supply the document that links them, such as a marriage or civil partnership certificate or a deed poll. If your address changed, give a note and evidence of the new address. If a document has expired, tell the team, since an expired passport may or may not be accepted for identity purposes depending on the department's rules, and a renewal can take weeks. If a document is lost or stolen, report it to the police or the issuer as appropriate, and tell the team, since you may be able to use a replacement or a different combination of documents. If you do not hold a passport or driving licence, ask what else is accepted. If you are a refugee or have no settled address, the team can often use alternative evidence, so explain your position. If a document has a mistake, for example a misspelled name, do not correct it yourself. Contact the issuer to have it corrected and tell the team. Never alter, borrow or use a document belonging to someone else. If you worry that someone has misused your identity, tell the team and the police, because it could affect checks. The way to handle each case is the same: be open, give the real evidence you have, and ask what else can be accepted. Departments want to confirm who you are, not to catch you out.

questions.prompt: Your passport shows your maiden name but you use your married name. What should you provide?

options.text: A new passport photograph with both names written on the back
The marriage certificate that links the two names
A signed letter from your line manager confirming the change
A handwritten note saying that the two names are the same person

questions.hint: An official document linking the names is the right evidence.

questions.prompt: Your passport has expired and a renewal will take weeks. What is best?

options.text: Send the expired passport without any comment and hope that it is accepted as it stands
Tell the team, since they will advise on what they can accept in the meantime
Alter the expiry date to match the renewal date
Wait until the renewed passport arrives before telling anyone

questions.hint: Rules vary, so the team should be told and asked.

questions.prompt: Your driving licence is stolen during the checks. What is the right step?

options.text: Ask a friend to lend you the same type of licence
Report the theft to the police or issuer and tell the checks team
Wait until the replacement arrives and mention it on your first day
Use a photocopy of the licence and tell nobody

questions.hint: Reporting protects you, and the team can suggest alternatives.

questions.prompt: Your birth certificate has your surname spelt wrongly. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore the mistake and hope that the checker does not notice
Contact the issuer to have it corrected and tell the checks team
Send the certificate with a note blaming the checker
Correct the spelling yourself in pen so it matches your passport

questions.hint: Do not alter documents. Get it corrected and keep the team informed.

questions.prompt: You are a refugee and have few documents. What should you do?

options.text: Explain your position to the team so alternative evidence can be agreed
Withdraw your application, because the check cannot be completed without a full set of papers
Wait to see whether the team asks you for anything
Use documents belonging to a family member who has a passport

questions.hint: Alternative evidence can often be accepted when circumstances are explained.

questions.prompt: A friend offers to lend you their utility bill so that you have address evidence. What is the right response?

options.text: Accept, and tell the checks team that it is a friend's bill
Accept, as long as you return it afterwards
Accept, but change the name so that it matches yours
Decline, since you must only use documents in your own name

questions.hint: Never use a document that belongs to someone else.

questions.prompt: You suspect that someone has used your identity to take out credit. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the evidence and hope the problem goes away without anyone finding out
Say nothing, because what happens to your identity outside work has nothing to do with the job
Tell the checks team and the police, because it could affect your checks
Wait until the credit agency contacts the department

questions.hint: Misuse of identity can show up in checks, so openness helps.

questions.prompt: The checks team asks for a document you do not have. Which approach fits the principles in this passage?

options.text: Send a different document without saying it is a substitute
Be open, give the real evidence you have, and ask what else can be accepted
Ask a referee to write a letter confirming your identity in place of the missing document
Make the missing document using a similar one as a template

questions.hint: Open communication and real evidence are the way forward.

questions.prompt: The checker says the photograph on your licence looks very different from you now. What is the best response?

options.text: Explain why, and offer another photo identity document if you have one
Say nothing and hope the checker accepts it
Ask the checker to ignore the photograph, as the name is correct
Bring a friend to confirm that the photograph is you

questions.hint: Be open and offer other evidence.

items.title: Level 5: History gaps and awkward references
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: The employment history check produces some of the trickiest situations because real lives are untidy. A few principles guide the answers. First, the whole period (usually three years) must be accounted for with a true description. Second, you should name someone or give a record that can confirm each period where you can. Third, if you cannot, say so honestly and offer another option rather than leaving a gap or inventing something. Fourth, a reference that is bad does not automatically end your chances. Departments look at the facts, and the BPSS is about verifying history. Fifth, if an employer gives only dates and job title, that is acceptable. Sixth, if you left a job under a cloud, for example after a dispute, give a short, calm and factual account and do not blame others. Seventh, if your history includes unpaid work, volunteering or caring, include it, since these are legitimate explanations. Eighth, if a job was short or ended quickly, list it anyway. Ninth, if you realise that you made a mistake in the dates after submitting the form, report it quickly. Finally, keep your own record of the information you provided, so that you give the same answers in every later form. These steps do not require you to have a perfect history. They require you to be accurate, consistent and open. Most problems arise not from the history itself, but from the attempt to hide or improve it.

questions.prompt: You were unemployed for eight months and living on savings. What is the best way to complete the form?

options.text: State that you were not working and say how you spent the time, with a contact if possible
List a short course that you only thought about taking
Leave the period blank, since there was no employer to name
Say you were self-employed, because that sounds better to the department than being out of work

questions.hint: The period must be accounted for with a true description.

questions.prompt: You cannot trace a manager from a job six years ago, but the job falls in the check period. What do you do?

options.text: Leave the job off the form because you cannot get a reference
Wait until the department asks about the missing referee
Give the name of a friend who once worked there and describe them as your manager
Say you cannot reach them and offer another way to confirm, such as payslips

questions.hint: Offer alternatives rather than leaving a gap or inventing a person.

questions.prompt: A former employer is likely to give a poor reference about your attendance. What is the best approach?

options.text: List a different employer name to avoid the reference, which you think could be poor
Ask the former employer to promise a good reference
List the job and, if asked, give a short factual account without blaming anyone
Leave the job off the form so that the employer is not contacted

questions.hint: Honesty and a calm account are better than concealment.

questions.prompt: An employer will only confirm dates and job title. Does this cause a problem?

options.text: It means the department will cancel the offer
It means you must provide a second employer to replace them
It is a failed check, since the reference was not full
It is acceptable, since the check is about verifying facts

questions.hint: Some employers have a policy of giving only bare facts.

questions.prompt: You volunteered for a charity for a year but were never paid. How should it appear on the form?

options.text: Include it as unpaid voluntary work, since it is a legitimate part of your history
Include it, but call it paid work to fit the form
Leave it off, since only paid jobs count
Include it only if the charity is registered abroad, because only overseas work needs to be listed

questions.hint: Volunteering is a valid account of how you spent the time.

questions.prompt: You left a job after a dispute. How should you describe it?

options.text: Say you left to pursue other interests, even if that is not true
Say nothing about the reason and leave the dates blank
Describe the manager in detail so the department understands your side
Give a short, calm and factual account without blaming others

questions.hint: Calm factual accounts are best.

questions.prompt: After sending your form you realise that one start date was two months wrong. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the checks team quickly and give the right date
Say nothing, because two months is unlikely to matter
Wait until a referee mentions the correct date
Change the date on your next form without telling the team

questions.hint: Correcting mistakes promptly shows honesty.

questions.prompt: Two forms you completed at different times give different dates for the same job. What is likely to happen?

options.text: The difference may be questioned, even if there is an innocent reason
The department will treat both dates as correct
The department will choose whichever of the two dates suits you best in the circumstances
The earlier date will be ignored without comment

questions.hint: Inconsistent answers raise questions, which is why records matter.

questions.prompt: You worked abroad for part of the period and cannot get a reference. What do you do?

options.text: Name a friend in the UK as your manager for that time
Say you were on a long holiday during that period
Explain where you worked, give dates and offer other evidence such as payslips or tax records
Leave that period blank, as the check only covers the UK

questions.hint: Offer other evidence rather than leaving a gap or inventing a person.

items.title: Level 5: Convictions on the form
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Questions about convictions cause worry, so it helps to apply a clear method. First, find out whether the conviction is spent or unspent for the type of post, using the checks team or an independent advice service rather than guessing. Second, answer the question as it is asked. If the form asks about unspent convictions and yours is spent, a standard post does not require you to declare it. If the post is an exempt one and the question covers spent convictions, you must answer in full. Third, if you have an unspent conviction, declare it and give a short, factual description, including the date and the outcome, without excuses or long stories. Fourth, tell the truth about any caution or similar outcome if the form asks. Fifth, if you are not sure how the form should be read, ask before you submit rather than after. Sixth, do not rely on an assumption that the department will not find out, because the records check is made through the official service. Seventh, if a charge is pending, ask the team how to proceed, since the position may differ from a conviction. Eighth, if your situation changes after you submit, such as a new charge or conviction, tell the department promptly. The department will look at the facts and decide fairly. A conviction does not automatically end an application, but a false answer to a question that you are required to answer will often do.

questions.prompt: You have a spent conviction and are applying for a standard post. The form asks only about unspent convictions. What do you do?

options.text: Declare it anyway, even though it is not asked for, and offer to resign if it causes a problem
Answer the question as asked, since a spent conviction need not be declared
Leave the form blank until you speak to a lawyer
Answer yes to the question to be on the safe side

questions.hint: For a standard post, spent convictions need not be declared.

questions.prompt: You have an unspent conviction from last year. How should you declare it?

options.text: Write a long story explaining why the court was wrong
Describe it as a caution rather than a conviction, to make the matter sound more minor
State only that you have had some problems in your past
Give a short, factual description with the date and the outcome

questions.hint: A clear, factual description is best.

questions.prompt: You are not sure whether the question includes cautions. What is the best step?

options.text: Submit the form and wait for them to raise it
Ask the checks team before you submit the form
Assume cautions never count and leave it out
Ask a friend in another department to read the form

questions.hint: Ask before submitting.

questions.prompt: A friend says the department will never find out about an old unspent conviction. What should you do?

options.text: Follow the advice and hope to be lucky
Ignore the advice, because the check is made through the official records service
Follow the advice only if the offence was a minor one
Follow the advice, as your friend probably knows how the records check works in practice

questions.hint: Records checks are official, so concealment is a poor strategy.

questions.prompt: You have been charged with an offence but not yet convicted. What do you do?

options.text: Say nothing, because you have not been convicted
Wait until the court case is over before telling anyone, since nothing has been decided yet
Ask the team how to proceed, as the position may differ from a conviction
Declare it as a conviction, as that is closest

questions.hint: A pending charge needs advice on how to proceed.

questions.prompt: After you submit your form, you receive a new conviction. What should you do?

options.text: Wait to see if the next check picks it up
Tell only your referees
Mention it at your first one-to-one
Tell the department promptly

questions.hint: Changes after submission need to be reported promptly.

questions.prompt: The post is described as exempt from the usual rules and the form asks about spent convictions. What do you do?

options.text: Skip the question and explain at interview
Answer in full, since the question covers spent convictions
Answer only about unspent convictions
Leave out spent convictions because the law normally protects them

questions.hint: Exempt posts can ask about spent convictions, so answer in full.

questions.prompt: Which approach carries the greatest risk to your application?

options.text: Giving a false answer to a question you are required to answer
Declaring a minor unspent conviction with a plain description
Asking the team how the form should be read
Taking independent advice about whether your conviction is spent

questions.hint: False answers damage trust more than most convictions.

questions.prompt: You declared an unspent conviction and the checks team asks for more details. What is the best response?

options.text: Reply only when they chase you a second time
Reply with a shorter account that leaves out the sentence
Reply that the matter is private and ask them to drop it
Reply promptly with a factual account and any court papers you have

questions.hint: Prompt, factual replies help the department decide fairly.

items.title: Level 5: Right to work and status changes
items.source: Home Office right to work guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Right to work issues depend on your own status, so the principle is to give accurate information and act early. Consider a few typical situations. If your visa will expire during employment, tell your employer well in advance and apply to renew in time, because an application made before the permission ends can often allow work to continue, but only if the correct checks confirm this. If you have applied to switch from a student route to a work route, ask your employer what evidence they need, as the rules depend on your category. If you receive settled status, naturalisation or a new passport, tell your employer so that its records are accurate. If you are asked for a share code, generate it from your own online account and share it only with the employer who needs it. If you have lost your documents, apply for replacements and tell the employer. If you are not sure whether you can start work before a decision, ask the recruitment team and the Home Office guidance rather than assume. Do not work in breach of your conditions, for example by exceeding limits on hours, as this can harm future applications. If your job offer relies on a particular status that then changes, discuss it early. Employers must carry out the checks properly and cannot employ someone without permission, so honest communication helps both sides find a lawful route.

questions.prompt: Your work visa expires in three months and you hold an offer for a role that continues beyond that. What is the best step?

options.text: Wait until the visa has expired and then explain what happened to your employer
Tell your employer well in advance and apply to renew in time
Apply for renewal only after the end date
Ask your colleagues to keep quiet about the date

questions.hint: Applying early and informing the employer is the lawful route.

questions.prompt: You have applied to extend your permission before it ends. What must the employer do before you carry on working?

options.text: Ask your line manager to approve a short extension to your right to work
End your contract until the decision arrives
Allow you to carry on working on your word alone
Carry out the correct check to confirm that you may continue to work

questions.hint: The employer must carry out the right check.

questions.prompt: You have received settled status. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it to yourself, because the old record is still valid
Tell only the bank and wait for them to inform your employer
Tell your employer so that its records are accurate
Wait until your next annual review

questions.hint: Accurate records protect both sides.

questions.prompt: You are asked for a share code. What is the right way to provide it?

options.text: Post it on a public forum so that anyone can check it for the employer
Let a friend generate it for you from their account
Share your login details instead of the code
Generate it from your own online account and give it only to the employer

questions.hint: A share code is created by you and given to the employer who needs it.

questions.prompt: You are not sure whether you can start work before a decision on a change of category. What do you do?

options.text: Assume it is fine, because the employer has made you an offer and will have checked the rules
Start work, and think about it afterwards
Ask a friend who has been through the same process
Ask the recruitment team and check Home Office guidance before you start

questions.hint: Do not assume. Check before working.

questions.prompt: You realise you have been working more hours than your conditions allow. What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing, since the employer has not complained about the hours you have been working
Ask a colleague to record fewer hours for you
Tell your employer and seek advice, as breaching conditions can harm future applications
Work fewer hours in future and hope that nobody notices

questions.hint: Do not hide a breach. Seek advice.

questions.prompt: You have lost your documents just before your start date. What should you do?

options.text: Apply for replacements and tell the employer straight away
Ask a referee to confirm your status
Delay telling the employer until you have the replacement documents in your hands
Use copies from an earlier job application

questions.hint: Early communication allows the employer to plan.

questions.prompt: Why does honest communication matter in these cases?

options.text: Employers can decide to ignore the rules if they like the worker
It allows the employer to keep the worker even if permission ends
It lets the employee avoid the right to work check
Employers cannot employ someone without permission, so it helps both sides find a lawful route

questions.hint: Both sides must act lawfully, and early talk helps.

questions.prompt: Your employer asks to see your documents again for a routine follow-up check. What do you do?

options.text: Ask them to rely on the earlier check and decline
Provide them but leave out anything that has changed
Provide them after your next holiday
Provide them promptly and tell the employer about any changes to your status

questions.hint: Follow-up checks are normal and part of the employer's duty.

items.title: Level 5: Reading eligibility in realistic cases
items.body: Eligibility questions are best handled with a short routine. Read the eligibility statement. Note who can apply, the clearance level, any residence period and any special conditions. Compare it with your own status, not with someone else's. If the advert is open to UK nationals only and you hold another nationality, you are not eligible for that post, but you may be eligible for others. If you hold dual nationality, check the statement and the contact point, as reserved posts may be more specific. If the advert is open to people with the right to work in the UK, your status must allow the work, and you will need to prove it. If a role needs a particular clearance, ask whether your residence history would be enough for the level, since a short period in the UK might delay or prevent vetting even though you meet the nationality rule. If your status is due to change, for example you are about to apply for citizenship, ask how the department would treat the application. Keep a note of the answers you get from the contact, including the date and the person's name. Do not apply on the basis of a friend's experience or a rumour. Do not hide a nationality or status to qualify, because the checks will reveal it and the dishonesty will end the process. If you are not eligible now, think about what would change that, such as time passing or a status change, and look out for future roles. Many entry-level jobs are open to a wide range of people.

questions.prompt: An advert is open to UK nationals only. You hold another nationality. What is your position?

options.text: You are not eligible for that post, but may be for others
You can apply, and the department will look at your case afterwards
You can apply if your application is strong enough
You can apply, provided you list only your UK links

questions.hint: The eligibility statement decides who can apply.

questions.prompt: You hold dual nationality and see a reserved post. What is the best step?

options.text: Check the statement and ask the contact point how it applies to you
Apply, and mention only the nationality that qualifies
Skip the post because you are sure that dual nationals are not eligible for reserved posts
Ask a friend with dual nationality what they did

questions.hint: Reserved posts can be specific, so ask.

questions.prompt: A role needs SC and you have lived in the UK only a short time. What is a sensible step?

options.text: Make the history look longer by changing the dates on the form so that it meets the level
Assume that the nationality rule is all that matters for the post and apply
Apply, and mention the residence history only if asked
Ask the contact whether your residence history would be enough for the level

questions.hint: Residence may limit vetting even if the nationality rule is met.

questions.prompt: You are about to apply for citizenship. What do you do?

options.text: Pretend you already hold citizenship
Ask the department how it would treat your application given the pending change
Wait until citizenship is granted and then apply, even if the post closes before that
Apply and write down a date for the grant

questions.hint: Ask, rather than assume.

questions.prompt: A friend says that a similar post was open to people with your status last year. What should you do?

options.text: Skip the post because rules are always tightened over time and it will be closed to you
Check the current eligibility statement, since the rules can change
Apply, since your friend has direct experience
Ask your friend to apply for you

questions.hint: Rules change, so rely on the current advert.

questions.prompt: You call the contact point about eligibility. What is a good habit?

options.text: Ask the contact to apply on your behalf
Note the date, the person's name and what you were told
Record nothing, because the answer will be in the advert
Share their name on social media

questions.hint: A note of the advice is useful if questions arise.

questions.prompt: Someone suggests leaving out your nationality on the form so that you qualify. What is wrong with this?

options.text: The checks will reveal it and the dishonesty will end the process
The department will accept any nationality if the application is strong
Nationality is not a required part of the checks
The form does not ask for it in any case

questions.hint: Concealment is dishonest and will be found out.

questions.prompt: You are not eligible now. What is a constructive step?

options.text: Ask your friends to apply for you
Apply for the same post again next week
Give up on the Civil Service entirely
Consider what might change this, such as time passing or a change in status, and watch for future roles

questions.hint: Many entry-level jobs are open to a wide range of people, and circumstances change.

questions.prompt: An advert is open to people with the right to work in the UK, and you hold time-limited permission to work. What should you do?

options.text: Apply and write that your permission has no end date
Explain your status and end date to the contact, then apply if it fits
Apply and say nothing about the end date
Skip the advert, because time-limited permission never counts

questions.hint: Be open about your status and ask when unsure.

items.title: Level 5: Matching the check to the role
items.body: Choosing the likely check for a role requires you to look at the sensitivity of the work, not the title. The general pattern is as follows. Roles that handle ordinary OFFICIAL information, such as processing claims, answering correspondence or maintaining records, usually need the BPSS only. Roles with some access to sensitive information or working near people or sites at risk, such as a post at a building that could be a terrorist target, may need a Counter-Terrorist Check. Roles that regularly handle SECRET information, or have frequent access to sensitive sites, usually need a Security Check. Roles with frequent and extensive access to TOP SECRET information, or in certain security and intelligence posts, usually need Developed Vetting. In each case the department decides, and the advert states the requirement. Several other features matter. Working in a team that supports a sensitive area does not by itself raise the level, since it depends on what you actually see. Short-term or temporary access can sometimes be managed under supervision without full clearance, though this is for the department to decide. A higher-level role may require you to hold the lower levels first. Taking a role with a lower requirement does not stop you moving to a higher one later, although you would then go through the extra checks. When you read an advert, ask yourself what you would see and where you would work. Then compare it with the stated requirement and ask the contact if it looks odd.

questions.prompt: A role processes benefit claims and answers customer letters. Which check does it most likely need?

options.text: Counter-Terrorist Check
Developed Vetting
The BPSS only
Security Check

questions.hint: Ordinary OFFICIAL work usually needs only the BPSS.

questions.prompt: A role is at a government building seen as a terrorist target, with no access to SECRET material. Which check is most likely?

options.text: Security Check
The BPSS only
Counter-Terrorist Check
Developed Vetting

questions.hint: CTC covers proximity to sites or people at risk and some access.

questions.prompt: A role regularly handles SECRET information. Which check is most likely?

options.text: Security Check
Counter-Terrorist Check
A basic criminal record check
The BPSS only

questions.hint: SC usually goes with regular SECRET access.

questions.prompt: A role has frequent and extensive access to TOP SECRET information. Which check is most likely?

options.text: The BPSS only
Security Check
Counter-Terrorist Check
Developed Vetting

questions.hint: DV is for frequent and extensive TOP SECRET access.

questions.prompt: You support a team that works on a sensitive area, but you only handle diaries and travel bookings. What decides your level?

options.text: The size of the building
What you actually see and do in the role
The name of the team you work in
The seniority of the people you support and the size of the team you join

questions.hint: The level depends on what you access, not the team name.

questions.prompt: An advert for an admin job asks for DV but the duties look ordinary. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Pass the advert to the Home Office
Ask the contact point to confirm the requirement
Apply and ask for DV to be removed afterwards
Assume the advert is wrong and apply for a lower level

questions.hint: If something looks odd, ask the contact.

questions.prompt: You take a BPSS-only role now. How does that affect applying for a higher-level role later?

options.text: You can apply later, but you would then go through the extra checks
You can move later, with no further checks needed
You can move only after serving for five years, and then with no further checks
You can never move to a higher level after joining

questions.hint: You can move later, with extra checks.

questions.prompt: Which question helps you when you read an advert?

options.text: How long is the job description?
What does the department's logo look like?
What would I see and where would I work?
How many people work in the department?

questions.hint: Sensitivity of access drives the level.

items.title: Level 5: Answering the security questionnaire
items.body: The security questionnaire asks about things people often find personal, so having a method helps. Use your own records to complete it. Make a list of your addresses and dates, employers, education, and close family. If you cannot remember a date, work it out from documents, such as old bank statements, tenancy agreements or payslips. If you are unsure of a detail, say so and give the best information you can. Be consistent with your earlier forms. If you have relatives abroad, list them honestly, because having relatives overseas is common and is not a reason for refusal in itself. If you have a partner, include their details as asked, since the form includes people close to you. Declare debts or financial difficulty at the level the form asks, and explain any plans. If you have used drugs or had other past difficulties, answer the question honestly according to the form's instructions, because vetting teams know that many people have a past. If a question seems intrusive, remember that the information is protected and used only for vetting. If you are unsure whether to include something, ask the department's security contact, who can advise without making a judgement. Save your draft and review it before you submit. Do not ask someone else to write the answers for you. If a referee is needed, ask them first, and give accurate contact details. Finally, if anything changes after you submit, tell the security contact so that the record stays accurate.

questions.prompt: You cannot remember when you moved into a flat three years ago. What is the best step?

options.text: Leave out the flat and fill the time with your previous address, so the history looks continuous
Ask a friend to guess the date
Work out the date from documents such as a tenancy agreement or bank statements
Choose a date that makes your address history look continuous

questions.hint: Documents give reliable dates.

questions.prompt: You have a sister living abroad. What do you do?

options.text: List her under a different relationship to avoid questions
Leave her off the form, because having contact abroad always causes refusal at any level
List her honestly, since relatives overseas are common and not a reason for refusal in themselves
Mention her only if asked in an interview

questions.hint: Honesty matters and relatives abroad are common.

questions.prompt: The form asks about your current partner. What is the right approach?

options.text: Leave them out because it is a private matter
Ask your partner to complete that section
Provide the details requested, since the form includes people close to you
Give partial details now and leave the rest of the information until a later date

questions.hint: The form covers close contacts.

questions.prompt: You owe money on a credit card and have a repayment plan. How should you handle the question about finances?

options.text: Leave out the debt and mention only the savings you have
Describe the debt as a business loan
Say that you have no debts and pay them off before the check
Declare the debt as the form asks and explain the plan

questions.hint: Declared debt with a plan shows responsibility.

questions.prompt: You have an old, minor drug offence that the form asks about. What do you do?

options.text: Write that you have never used any drugs
Ask a friend whether they would declare it, and do as they would
Leave it out, since it was a long time ago
Answer honestly according to the instructions on the form

questions.hint: Vetting teams know many people have a past, and honesty is expected.

questions.prompt: A question seems very intrusive. What is the best response?

options.text: Remember the information is protected and used only for vetting, and ask the security contact if unsure
Skip the question because it is too personal
Answer with general comments that avoid the specifics, because the question seems intrusive
Ask your referee whether you need to answer

questions.hint: The security contact can advise and the data is protected.

questions.prompt: A friend offers to complete your questionnaire quickly. What should you do?

options.text: Accept if they are a civil servant
Accept the offer of help if you check their draft carefully afterwards
Accept if they promise to be accurate
Decline, since the answers must be yours and be true

questions.hint: Do not ask others to write your answers.

questions.prompt: After submitting the questionnaire, you change address. What should you do?

options.text: Resubmit the questionnaire from the start
Do nothing at all, because the form has already been submitted and cannot be changed
Tell the security contact so that the record stays accurate
Update your address only with your bank

questions.hint: Changes after submission should be reported.

questions.prompt: Your address history has gaps because you stayed with friends for a while. What is the best approach?

options.text: Ask the vetting team to skip the address section
List where you stayed with approximate dates and offer a contact who can confirm it
List an invented address to fill the time
List only your last permanent address and ignore the gaps

questions.hint: Gaps are explained honestly with a contact who can confirm.

questions.prompt: You are told to share your vetting form with a friend who has been through the process. What should you do?

options.text: Decline, since the form is personal and your answers must be your own
Share it, but remove your name
Share it only after you have submitted it
Share it, as a friend can spot mistakes

questions.hint: The questionnaire is confidential and personal.

items.title: Level 5: Delays, refusals and appeals
items.body: Not every clearance case goes smoothly, and it helps to know the sensible responses. If the process is slow, check that you have completed everything asked of you, and then ask the department's security contact for an update, as they can contact the vetting team on your behalf. If you are asked for more information, reply quickly and fully. If you are asked to explain something in your background, do so truthfully and with evidence where possible, such as bank statements showing a repayment plan. If you are interviewed, prepare by reviewing your form, and answer calmly and honestly. Do not try to guess what the interviewer wants. If clearance is delayed, you may be able to start in a role with limited access, or in a different role, if the department allows. Ask your manager or HR what is possible, but do not assume it. If clearance is refused, you will be told, and you can ask for the decision to be reviewed through the department's process. There is also an independent appeal route. A refusal at one level does not stop you applying for jobs that need a lower level or none, and some people can be cleared later if their circumstances change. Whatever happens, protect your confidentiality: do not discuss the details of your vetting widely and do not contact referees to ask them what they told the team. Use official channels, keep records of correspondence, and consider independent advice if you want to challenge a decision.

questions.prompt: Your clearance has taken longer than you expected. What is the best first step?

options.text: Contact your referees and ask them to chase the vetting team for a faster decision
Check you have completed everything and ask the security contact for an update
Resign and apply again for a lower level
Send daily emails to the vetting team

questions.hint: The security contact can ask the vetting team on your behalf.

questions.prompt: The vetting team asks you to explain a past debt. What should you do?

options.text: Say that someone else was responsible for the debt, even if the account is in your name
Wait to see if the question is asked again
Explain truthfully and provide evidence such as statements showing a repayment plan
Reply that the debt is no longer relevant

questions.hint: Truthful explanation with evidence helps.

questions.prompt: You are invited to a vetting interview. How should you prepare?

options.text: Ask your referees to attend with you
Memorise a short script
Review your form and answer calmly and honestly
Learn what interviewers usually want to hear and aim your answers at it

questions.hint: Honest and consistent answers are best.

questions.prompt: Clearance is delayed and you have already been offered the job. What may be possible?

options.text: Starting after resigning from your current job
Starting immediately without any checks
Starting in a role with limited access, if the department allows it
Starting with full access to sensitive material, since the offer has already been made

questions.hint: This is not guaranteed and is for the department to decide.

questions.prompt: Your clearance is refused. What are your options?

options.text: Apply again straight away for the same role
Accept it, since a decision on clearance is always final once it is made
Ask for a review through the department's process, and use the independent appeal route if needed
Contact your referees and ask them to change what they said

questions.hint: Review and appeal routes exist.

questions.prompt: Does a refusal at one level stop you applying for other jobs?

options.text: It applies only to jobs in the same department
It does not stop you applying for jobs that need a lower level or none
It bars you from government jobs at any level for a period of five years
It bars you from all government jobs for life

questions.hint: Many jobs need less or no clearance.

questions.prompt: What should you do about what your referees told the vetting team?

options.text: Contact them politely, as it is only a conversation
Contact them to ask what they said so that you can correct anything
Use official channels and keep the matter confidential
Contact them by post, so there is a record

questions.hint: Contacting referees about their input is not appropriate.

questions.prompt: How can you protect your position if you want to challenge a decision?

options.text: Keep records of correspondence and consider independent advice
Discuss the case widely so others can advise you
Contact the vetting staff directly at their homes to put your case
Post the case online

questions.hint: Records and advice help.

items.title: Level 5: Security habits in real situations
items.body: Security training makes more sense when you apply it to realistic situations. A new starter is likely to meet some of these. A person you do not recognise follows you through a secure door. Politely ask who they are and to use their own pass, or point them to reception. If they cannot show a pass, tell security. A colleague asks to borrow your pass because they have forgotten theirs. Decline and send them to reception, since passes are personal. You find a USB stick in the car park. Do not plug it in, because it may carry malware. Give it to the security team. You receive an email asking you to click a link to reset your password. Do not click. Check with IT and report it as suspected phishing. You have a call with a customer and realise that you are in a busy cafe. End the call or move to a private place, since you may be overheard. You have a document printed and left it on the printer for an hour. Report this to your line manager, since someone might have seen it. You notice a colleague looking at records they do not need. Report your concern through the proper route. You lose your laptop or phone on a train. Report it at once so that access can be blocked. You want to work from home. Use only approved equipment and follow the rules for secure remote working. In every case, reporting early is more important than blame. Security teams rely on people telling them quickly so that harm can be limited.

questions.prompt: A stranger follows you through a secure door without using a pass. What is the best response?

options.text: Hold the door for them and say nothing
Politely ask who they are and to use their own pass, or point them to reception
Ignore it, since they look like they work in the building and are probably staff
Challenge them loudly in front of everyone

questions.hint: Politely challenging is expected.

questions.prompt: A colleague has forgotten their pass and asks to borrow yours. What do you do?

options.text: Decline and direct them to reception
Lend it if they are in the same team
Lend it for the morning and ask for it back
Lend it, but go in with them

questions.hint: Passes are personal.

questions.prompt: You find a USB stick in the car park. What should you do?

options.text: Plug it in to see whose it is
Hand it to the security team without plugging it in
Take it home to check what is on it using your own computer
Leave it where it is

questions.hint: Unknown devices may carry malware.

questions.prompt: You receive an unexpected email asking you to click a link to reset your password. What is the best step?

options.text: Forward the email to all colleagues as a warning
Reply to ask the sender if it is genuine
Do not click, check with IT and report it as suspected phishing
Click the link and enter your password to avoid being locked out

questions.hint: Suspected phishing should be reported.

questions.prompt: You are on a call with a customer and realise that you are in a busy cafe. What is best?

options.text: Move to a private place or end the call
Carry on, since nobody is listening
Write the customer's details on a napkin
Lower your voice and carry on

questions.hint: You may be overheard in public.

questions.prompt: A confidential document you printed has been left on the printer for an hour. What should you do?

options.text: Wait to see if anyone mentions it
Say nothing, since the document is back in your hands and nothing seems to be missing
Throw it in the nearest bin
Report it to your line manager, since someone might have seen it

questions.hint: Report possible exposure.

questions.prompt: You notice a colleague looking at records they do not appear to need. What is the right step?

options.text: Say nothing, because it is not your responsibility
Report your concern through the proper route
Look at the same records to compare
Confront them in front of the team

questions.hint: Concerns should be reported.

questions.prompt: You lose your work phone on a train. What should you do?

options.text: Report it at once so access can be blocked
Wait a few days to see if it is found
Report it only if you stored passwords on it
Buy a replacement and say nothing

questions.hint: Early reports limit harm.

items.title: Level 5: Handling personal data in practice
items.source: Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR; GOV.UK
items.body: Data protection rules come alive in everyday decisions. A few principles guide them: use data only for the purpose it was collected for, look only at what you need, share only with those entitled to see it, keep it secure, and report problems. Imagine you work in a team handling customer records. A friend asks you to check whether their claim has been paid. You should not look at the record. Direct them to the official route to ask. You realise that you sent an email with a customer's details to the wrong address. Tell your line manager or the data protection team at once, and if you can, ask the recipient to delete it. A caller says they are a customer's relative and asks for information. Do not give details unless identity and entitlement are checked under the procedure. You see a record for a person you know. Do not read it unless your task needs it, and consider telling your manager so someone else can deal with the case. You want to take paperwork home to finish a task. Check the rules first, since you may not be allowed to. A manager asks you to copy a list of customers to a personal device. Politely decline and ask about approved methods. A customer asks to see the information held about them. This is a subject access request. Pass it to the team that handles them, since there are legal time limits. The basic habit is to pause and ask whether you are entitled to do something before you do it, and to tell someone quickly if something goes wrong.

questions.prompt: A friend asks you to check whether their claim has been paid. What do you do?

options.text: Decline to look and direct them to the official route
Look, and tell them what you see
Look quickly, since you are only reading the record and not changing anything
Ask a colleague to look instead

questions.hint: Looking without a work reason is a breach.

questions.prompt: You sent an email with a customer's details to the wrong address. What is the best step?

options.text: Delete the sent message to hide it
Send another email with a different subject line, asking them to ignore the first
Wait to see whether the recipient responds
Tell your line manager or the data protection team at once

questions.hint: Quick reports limit harm.

questions.prompt: A caller claims to be a customer's relative and asks for information. What should you do?

options.text: Give details if they know the address
Give limited details to be helpful
Give details if they sound sure
Check identity and entitlement under the procedure before giving anything

questions.hint: Information is only for entitled people.

questions.prompt: You see the record of someone you know in a case you did not expect. What is best?

options.text: Read it all, to make sure you understand the case before you decide what to do
Delete the record to protect them
Avoid reading it unless needed and consider telling your manager so someone else handles it
Tell your friend that you saw their record

questions.hint: Avoid conflicts and unnecessary access.

questions.prompt: You want to take paperwork home to finish a task. What should you do?

options.text: Take it, as long as you bring it back
Email the contents to your personal address so that you can work on it at home
Check the rules first, since you may not be allowed to
Photograph the pages to take home

questions.hint: Rules limit removal of papers.

questions.prompt: A manager asks you to copy a customer list to a personal device. What is the right response?

options.text: Do it, but only copy half of the list so that less is at risk
Do it, but delete the file later
Do it, because the manager asked
Politely decline and ask about approved methods

questions.hint: Personal devices are not approved.

questions.prompt: A customer asks to see the information held about them. What should you do?

options.text: Ask them to write to the minister
Tell them it is not allowed
Print what you can find and give it to them, as it is their own information
Pass it to the team that handles these requests, since there are time limits

questions.hint: This is a subject access request.

questions.prompt: What is the basic habit that helps most in data protection?

options.text: Pause and ask whether you are entitled to do something before you do it
Copy data to make a backup for yourself
Share information with anyone in the same team who asks you for it
Work as quickly as you can and fix any mistakes later on

questions.hint: Think before acting.

items.title: Level 5: Conflicts, gifts and social media
items.body: The Civil Service Code is easiest to understand when applied to everyday dilemmas. Suppose your brother runs a company that applies to supply your department. Declare the relationship to your manager at once and take no part in the decision. Suppose a supplier sends you a hamper at the end of a contract. Gifts that could influence decisions should be declined or handed in, and offers are recorded, so check your department's rules. Suppose a supplier invites you to lunch while a tender is open. Decline or check the rules, because hospitality during a live process looks improper. Suppose a friend asks you to put in a word for their application. Do not use your position to help them, and declare the link if it could affect a decision. Suppose a colleague posts strong political opinions on social media and identifies as a civil servant. Civil servants must stay politically impartial, and the posts could harm trust. You might raise it politely with them or your manager. Suppose you see an error that could cost the public money. Report it, even if it embarrasses someone. Suppose your manager asks you to do something you think is wrong. Raise your concern first with the manager. If that does not work, use the department's routes or the Civil Service Commission. Suppose you plan to take a second job. Check the rules on outside work, since you may need approval. Whenever you are unsure, ask, record your decision and act in the open.

questions.prompt: Your brother runs a company that applies to supply your department. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a colleague to help him quietly
Say nothing unless his company wins
Help him write a strong bid
Declare the relationship to your manager and take no part in the decision

questions.hint: Declare and step back.

questions.prompt: A supplier sends you a gift hamper at the end of a contract. What is the best response?

options.text: Keep it only if it is worth little
Share it with your team and say nothing
Decline or hand it in, record the offer and follow your department's rules
Keep it, since the contract has finished and the supplier cannot be influenced now

questions.hint: Gifts that could influence decisions are declined.

questions.prompt: A supplier invites you to lunch while a tender is open. What is best?

options.text: Decline or check the rules, since hospitality during a live process looks improper
Accept, but do not discuss the tender
Accept, and tell your manager about the lunch afterwards
Accept, as long as you split the bill

questions.hint: Avoid hospitality during live processes.

questions.prompt: A friend asks you to put in a word for their application. What do you do?

options.text: Do not use your position to help and declare the link if it could affect a decision
Pass them the questions in advance
Say yes but do not tell anyone
Put in a word for them, since it is only a small favour between friends

questions.hint: Using your position for others is improper.

questions.prompt: A colleague posts strong political opinions and identifies as a civil servant. What is a sensible response?

options.text: Raise it politely with them or with your manager, since impartiality matters
Share the posts to show support
Report them to the newspaper
Ignore it, since what people post on their own social media is private

questions.hint: Impartiality protects trust.

questions.prompt: You see an error that could cost the public money. What do you do?

options.text: Fix it quietly yourself without telling anyone, so that no one is embarrassed
Wait to see whether it is noticed
Tell the supplier and ask them to correct it
Report it, even if it is embarrassing for someone

questions.hint: Reporting is the right course.

questions.prompt: Your manager asks you to do something you think is wrong. What is the right sequence?

options.text: Do it, then complain afterwards
Raise your concern with the manager, then use the department's routes or the Civil Service Commission if needed
Tell the press first
Refuse and leave the building

questions.hint: Raise concerns through proper routes.

questions.prompt: You plan to take a second job outside work. What should you do?

options.text: Start it and tell nobody
Check the rules on outside work, since you may need approval
Ask your colleagues for permission
Start it, since the hours of the second job are completely separate from your own

questions.hint: Outside work may need approval.

items.title: Level 5: Early-weeks judgement calls
items.body: The first weeks bring many small decisions where judgement counts. These principles apply. Ask when unsure: it is better to ask than to guess, particularly about security, data and conduct. Be honest about mistakes: say so early. Keep confidences, including at home and online. Use official systems and do not use personal accounts for work. Record what you do so that you can explain it later. Follow instructions from your manager unless they would break the law or the Code, and raise concerns if they do. Look after your own wellbeing, because stress can lead to mistakes, and use the support on offer, including the employee assistance programme and your manager. Use the probation period to ask for feedback and to say what help you need, such as reasonable adjustments. Build relationships, but keep boundaries on what you share. Take mandatory learning seriously. Notice what is normal in the team and ask about anything that seems out of line. Avoid gossip about colleagues or customers. Keep your pass and equipment safe. If you are asked to take on something beyond your skills, say what you can do and what you need to learn. Do not pretend to know. Check that deadlines are realistic and flag problems early. Finally, remember that you are trusted with a public service. How you behave in small matters shows whether you can be trusted with larger ones. People who ask questions, tell the truth and learn from errors are usually the ones who do well.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether you can share some customer information with another team. What should you do?

options.text: Wait for the other team to ask twice
Share it, but mark it as confidential
Ask your manager or the security team before sharing
Share it, because both teams work for the same department

questions.hint: It is better to ask than to guess.

questions.prompt: You realise you made an error in a document that has already gone to a customer. What is best?

options.text: Tell your manager quickly so the error can be put right
Hide the original so that there is no evidence of the mistake
Send a new copy without comment
Wait to see whether the customer notices

questions.hint: Early honesty about mistakes is best.

questions.prompt: You are tempted to use your personal email to finish some work faster. What should you do?

options.text: Use your personal email, but delete the messages afterwards
Use your personal email for non-sensitive files only
Use only the official systems, even if it takes longer
Use your personal email, but tell nobody

questions.hint: Official systems keep information protected.

questions.prompt: Your manager asks you to do a task that would break the law. What do you do?

options.text: Raise your concern and, if needed, use the department's routes
Do it, because you were told to
Do it, but keep a private copy of the instructions in case you are blamed
Refuse without giving a reason

questions.hint: Instructions do not override the law or the Code.

questions.prompt: You feel overwhelmed in your third week. What is a sensible step?

options.text: Complain about your colleagues to the rest of the team
Talk to your manager and use the support on offer
Say nothing and try to work harder
Take a week off without telling anyone

questions.hint: Support exists and stress can lead to mistakes.

questions.prompt: You are asked to take on a task beyond your current skills. What should you do?

options.text: Accept and try to hide any gaps
Refuse the task altogether
Say what you can do and what you need to learn
Pass it to a colleague without explaining why you cannot do it

questions.hint: Do not pretend to know.

questions.prompt: A colleague gossips about a customer's personal circumstances. What is best?

options.text: Avoid joining in, and raise it with your manager if it continues
Join in, since it is only chat
Repeat it to other teams
Post it online to ask other people for advice about how to react

questions.hint: Customers' information must stay confidential.

questions.prompt: Why do small matters count for your reputation?

options.text: Small matters are checked once a year
Small matters decide your pay band
Small matters are the only ones that your manager ever notices or records
How you behave in small matters shows whether you can be trusted with larger ones

questions.hint: Trust is built from small actions.
